newsitem.title: INDIA: More than 460 killed in Indian cyclone.
newsitem.headline: More than 460 killed in Indian cyclone.

text.p: A cyclone has killed more than 460 people in India's major crop-growing state of Andhra Pradesh, state police officials said on Thursday.
"The rice bowl of the state looks like a burial ground," Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister V. Chandrababu Naidu, told reporters after he surveyed the flood-hit areas by helicopter.

Naidu said the death toll might climb to 1,000 and he had appealed to the federal government of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda to treat the incident as a "national calamity" and sanction special relief funds.

The storm, with winds of between 100 and 120 kmph (60 and 75 mph), struck India's southeast coast near the port of Kakinada on Wednesday, flattening homes, destroying crops and cutting transport and communication links. But it weakened on Thursday.
"The port is paralysed and no work is being done," said Satyanarayana Reddy, a businessman from Kakinada. "We do not know what has been the fate of ships anchored at the port.
"It's a terrible sight in the city. Winds uprooted most electrical poles which are lying twisted on the ground. There is no power. Roads have been blocked and coconut groves heavily damaged."
Authorities in Hyderabad, the capital of Andhra Pradesh, said most of the deaths were due to flooding, houses collapsing and electrocutions.
"The death toll is now 465," said a state police official who did not want to be identified. "It is rising every hour."
"This is the worst cyclone in 10 years," H.S. Brahma, the state official in charge of relief operations told Reuters.
The cyclone crossed the coast 50 km (30 miles) south of Kakinada. It tore down power and telephone lines, and wreaked havoc in the rich rice-growing Godavari river delta, officials said.
In East Godavari, where 100,000 homes were destroyed or damaged, at least 309 people have died. Authorities said 42 of them were killed when a boat capsized in the Godavari river.

"We have not been able to communicate with Kakinada or reach that place which is only 40 km (25 miles) from Rajahmundry," Arun Kumar, a resident of Rajahmundry, a major town in East Godavari, told Reuters by telephone.
"We had a six-hour downpour accompanied by heavy winds last night," Kumar said. Hundreds of massive trees had collapsed and the town lay paralysed without power, he said.
Nearly 200,000 people were evacuated from their homes and moved to higher ground after water levels rose two metres (six feet) in coastal areas, officials said.

The floods washed away the standing rice crop over an area of 8.5 million hectares (22 million acres), Doordarshan said. Another 1.9 million hectares (4.8 million acres) of cultivable land was also swamped, it said.
"There has been large scale damage of plantation crops -- mostly coconut and bananas, and other horticultural produce," Brahma said.
Port officials in Kakinada said three ships appeared to have been washed ashore in the storm. They had no details.

The cyclone appeared to be petering out. "The system (depression) is weakening," C.V.V. Bhadram, director of the Meteorological Centre, said. It had moved deeper inland and would head in a west-northwest direction, he said.

Businesses, offices, and schools have been shut till Sunday. The government has asked the military to help with relief operations. The district administration is providing grain and drinking water to all those who lost their homes, accommodated in 178 relief camps.
Andhra Pradesh, particularly vulnerable to cyclones because of its flat coast, saw 967 people die in a 1990 cyclone that left 22 billion rupees ($650 million) worth of damage in its wake.
But more than 10,000 people died in the worst cyclone, in November 1977. It disrupted life for 5.4 million people and set off a 15-metre tidal wave that swept 12 km (7 miles) inland.
